source.title: Understanding SAM's Robustness to Noisy Labels through Gradient Down-weighting
source.authors: Hoang-Chau Luong; Quang-Thuc Nguyen; D. Tran; Minh-Triet Tran

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies SAM and noisy-label memorization. Its experiments do not test the listed claims about fitting random labels alongside generalizing on natural labels, or the listed architecture, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness, and memorized-example claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on training with corrupted labels, which is distinct from the claim versions' settings and measures. These related findings are recorded under fits_no_version; cited results from other studies are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures SAM's gradient down-weighting and noisy-label robustness, then evaluates SANER. None of its results tests V1–V8. Partial label corruption does not establish V1's random-label/natural-label comparison; widening regularized ResNets for 200 epochs does not establish V2's post-interpolation trend under training to convergence. SAM optimization and perturbation-radius comparisons do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–gap correlation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors identify element-wise gradient down-weighting, supported by stronger amplification of clean gradients, as a mechanism slowing noisy-label memorization during the transitional phase. They conclude that SANER strengthens this mechanism and improves noisy-label performance across their tested settings, while performing on par with SAM on clean data. Their theory concerns linear models; deep-network evidence is empirical.
record.recipe_differences: Studies SAM's element-wise gradient behavior and proposes SANER in label-noise settings; it does not reproduce the listed claim versions' methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Label-noise rate and type, dataset, architecture, model width, training time, and SAM perturbation radius are varied in the paper.

fits_no_version.finding: Under 50% symmetric CIFAR-10 label noise, SAM down-weights 35–45% of gradient elements across three architectures; their alignment with noisy-example gradients rises during training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM selectively reduces gradient components associated with noisy-label updates.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing SAM's down-weighted gradient elements with SGD counterparts raises final noisy-label accuracy from approximately 30% to nearly 80%, while clean-sample accuracy remains comparable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM's element-wise down-weighting contributes to slower noisy-label memorization.

fits_no_version.finding: With wider ResNet18 models on corrupted CIFAR-100, SAM's noisy fitting approaches SGD's, whereas SANER slows noisy fitting and retains better test performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SANER can preserve noise robustness when increasing model width under the tested fixed training budget.

fits_no_version.finding: On clean CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, SANER achieves test accuracy close to SAM's; the authors describe no noticeable improvement.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SANER preserves SAM's clean-data accuracy in the tested settings.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS) 2026, as stated in the supplied text
record.problems: Theoretical analysis is for linear models; the empirical experiments concern label noise. Some training-curve outcomes are described in text or figures without exact numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports further SANER-versus-SAM test-accuracy comparisons across datasets, noise types, architectures, optimizer variants, noise-robust strategies, and perturbation radii (Tables 1–5 and 7; Figures 3–5 and 7). These are comparisons of the proposed noisy-label method and do not directly test a listed claim version, so they are not included as rows.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fully random labels alongside natural-label generalization using the same architecture and recipe, including chance-level held-out accuracy with random labels.
Test-error trends beyond the width needed for zero training error in networks trained to convergence without explicit regularization.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity or convolution-derived initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD under limited or broader tuning, including weight-decay and optimizer-switching conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and changes from adapted training recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out error, including dataset-size, dropout-strength, and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance as a correlate and ranking measure of generalization gaps among similarly fitted networks.
Retraining after removing examples selected by label-memorization influence, compared with removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The cannot_determine states concern the listed claim versions, not whether the unrelated findings occurred. No claim-version verdict is warranted. Other method-performance comparisons are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels under the listed recipes.
Width beyond the zero-training-error threshold on natural labels.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks on images.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD under the stated tuning conditions.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a correlate of the generalization gap.

rows.subject: ResNet18 (RN18)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of gradient elements down-weighted by SAM relative to SGD during noisy-label training.
rows.measure: Percentage of gradient elements with 0 < SAM/SGD gradient ratio < 1
rows.note: Reported across three architectures; this row records the RN18 result only insofar as the text provides a pooled range, not a separate RN18 value.
rows.check: The 35–45% range is reported across ResNet18, WideResNet40-2, and DenseNet121, not as a separate ResNet18 estimate. The gradient statistic measures no listed version.

rows.subject: ResNet18 (RN18)
rows.operation_detail: Measured cosine similarity between the SGD gradient on SAM-down-weighted elements and the SGD gradient on noisy examples.
rows.note: The text describes a peak over time, not an exact point estimate.
rows.check: The approximately 0.7 peak is described for Figure 2b, which contains three architectures; the prose does not establish this as a separate ResNet18 estimate. Gradient alignment measures no listed version.

rows.subject: ResNet18 (RN18)
rows.operation_detail: Replaced SAM gradient elements in the down-weighted set with their SGD counterparts (SGD-D).
rows.note: The paper says SGD-D accelerates noisy-label memorization; clean-sample performance remains comparable to SAM.
rows.check: The nearly 80% versus approximately 30% noisy-label accuracy comparison is supported. This is an optimizer-update ablation, not a direct weight edit. Neither this noisy-subset fitting measure nor comparable clean-training accuracy establishes V1.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Increased model width in an overfitting-prone noisy-label setting.
rows.measure: Noisy-label fitting rate and test accuracy
rows.baseline: The text says SAM matches SGD's noisy fitting rate as width increases.
rows.value: SANER maintains a slower noisy fitting rate and achieves higher test accuracy.
rows.note: This is a noisy-label result and does not establish the listed natural-label width claim.
rows.check: Combines two widths, noisy-label fitting, and test accuracy into one row and primarily compares the proposed method with baselines. Figure 6 supports the qualitative statement, but no zero-training-error threshold or convergence is established. Weight decay, augmentation, and a fixed 200-epoch budget also differ from V2.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Compared SGD, SAM, and SANER on clean datasets without label noise.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation over three runs with different random seeds
rows.note: The authors characterize SANER as on par with SAM in clean settings, without noticeable improvement.
rows.check: Table 6 values are correct, but this is the proposed method's performance comparison, not a listed-claim result. It combines two datasets; the reported statistic is best test accuracy over training, summarized across three seeds. The operation mentions SGD but omits its values: 95.18±0.09 and 78.06±0.09.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
